extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate/graduate mathematics students and mathematicians interested in elegant elementary proofs and classical problem solutions
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and standards for producing elementary, rigorous proofs in number theory, analysis, and geometry (irrationality proofs, evaluation of series/integrals, and polyhedral decomposition arguments). Emphasizes choosing substitutions, constructing auxiliary polynomials, use of integrals/estimates, parity/valuation tricks, and combinatorial linear-algebra arguments for decompositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polar form and nth roots of unity
rubrics_metrics.description: complex number z = x + iy may be written in the “polar” form z = r e^{iϕ} = r(cos ϕ + i sin ϕ), where r = |z| = sqrt(x^2 + y^2) and ϕ is the angle measured from the positive x-axis; the n-th roots of unity are therefore of the form λ_k = e^{2kπi/n} = cos(2kπ/n) + i sin(2kπ/n), 0 ≤ k ≤ n−1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use polar representation for geometric interpretation (inscribe regular n-gon in unit circle), to parametrize roots of unity and to exploit multiplicative/group structure (roots form cyclic group {ζ, ζ^2, …, ζ^n = 1}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and factorization via cyclotomic polynomials φ_d(x)
rubrics_metrics.description: Group all roots of order d together and set φ_d(x) := ∏_{λ of order d} (x − λ). Since every root has some order d, xn − 1 = ∏_{d|n} φ_d(x). The definition of φ_d(x) is independent of n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this factorization to reduce statements about xn − 1 to properties of the φ_d(x); treat φ_d as intrinsic cyclotomic polynomials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrality and constant term ±1 of φ_n(x)
rubrics_metrics.description: The coefficients of the polynomials φ_n(x) are integers (φ_n(x) ∈ Z[x] for all n), and the constant coefficient is either 1 or −1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by induction: base case φ_1(x)=x−1; assume φ_d ∈ Z[x] with constant term ±1 for d<n; write xn −1 = p(x) φ_n(x) and compare coefficients. Use that p0 = ±1 to deduce constant term and integrality of successive coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisibility relations from cyclotomic factorization
rubrics_metrics.description: From factorization and specialization at q one gets φ_n(q) | q^n − 1 and φ_n(q) | q^{nk} − 1; combining class formula relations yields φ_n(q) | q − 1 (which may lead to contradiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use algebraic divisibility from factorization plus number-theoretic class formulas; then combine with analytic/absolute-value estimates on |q − λ| to obtain contradictions when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use absolute-value bounds on |q − λ| to rule out divisibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If λ is an n-th root of unity with real part a < 1, then |q − λ|^2 = q^2 − 2aq + 1 > (q − 1)^2, hence |q − λ| > q − 1; consequently |φ_n(q)| = ∏_λ |q − λ| > (q − 1) and so φ_n(q) cannot divide q − 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine explicit lower bounds on factors |q − λ| with divisibility relations to derive contradictions; this is a standard way to show impossibility of certain algebraic integers dividing small integers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiply-by-n! trick for proving e irrational
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume e = a/b rational. Substitute the series e = Σ_{k≥0} 1/k! and multiply by n!; separate the finite integral part n!b Σ_{k=0}^n 1/k! (integer) from the remainder n!b Σ_{k=n+1}^� 1/k!, which lies strictly between b/(n+1) and b/n, so cannot be integer for large n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose n large so remainder is strictly between 0 and 1 (or not an integer), yielding contradiction. This simple 'multiply-by-n!' idea underlies many elementary irrationality proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liouville variant / parity trick for e^2 irrationality
rubrics_metrics.description: Write be = a e^{−1} (or similarly for e^2) and substitute series expansions for e and e^{-1}; multiply by a suitably chosen large even n to make integer parts large and the alternating remainder small but of opposite sign, giving a contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two 'tricks' combine: use alternating series for e^{-1} and parity choices of n (even) to force the remainder signs to contradict equality. This is a refinement of the multiply-by-n! method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Legendre's theorem on 2-adic valuation of n!
rubrics_metrics.description: For any n ≥ 1 the integer n! contains the prime factor 2 at most n−1 times, with equality iff n is a power of two (n=2^m).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to choose n = 2^m to maximize the power of 2 dividing n!, and when proving irrationality of e^{2} or e^{4} multiply by n!/2^{n−1} (or similar) to ensure denominators are controlled and summands become even/integer as required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct auxiliary polynomial f(x)=x^n(1-x)^n / n! with integrality properties
rubrics_metrics.description: For fixed n ≥ 1, f(x) = x^n(1−x)^n / n! is a polynomial of the form (1/n!) 2^n Σ_{i=n}^{2n} c_i x^i with integer coefficients; for 0 < x < 1 we have 0 < f(x) < 1/n!; and all derivatives f^{(k)}(0) and f^{(k)}(1) are integers for k ≥ 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lemma supplies a compactly supported polynomial with small values on (0,1) and integer boundary derivatives—perfect for constructing linear combinations of derivatives whose boundary values are integers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct F(x) as alternating linear combination of derivatives to produce integer boundary values
rubrics_metrics.description: Define F(x) := s^{2n} f(x) − s^{2n−1} f'(x) + s^{2n−2} f''(x) ∓ ... (finite sum). Then F'(x) = −s F(x) + s^{2n+1} f(x) and d/dx [e^{s x} F(x)] = s^{2n+1} e^{s x} f(x). Integrating yields N = b ∫_0^1 s^{2n+1} e^{s x} f(x) dx = aF(1) − bF(0), an integer, but estimates make 0 < N < 1 for large n, contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick n large (explicit bounds: n! > a s^{2n+1}) so that the integral N is nonzero but <1; by (iii) boundary derivatives are integers, hence N integer; contradiction proves irrationality of e^s for rational s.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous F(x) construction for π^2 irrationality using trigonometric integration
rubrics_metrics.description: Define F(x) := b n (π^{2n} f(x) − π^{2n−2} f^{(2)}(x) + π^{2n−4} f^{(4)}(x) ∓ ...). One shows d/dx (F'(x) sin πx − π F(x) cos πx) = π^2 a n f(x) sin πx so N := π ∫_0^1 a n f(x) sin πx dx = F(0) + F(1) is integer, yet for n large 0 < N < 1, contradiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lemma properties of f(x) and choose n so π a n / n! < 1; the trigonometric identity and boundary integrality produce a contradiction proving π^2 irrational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cosine addition theorem to derive integer recurrence for cos kϕ
rubrics_metrics.description: Addition theorem cos(α+β) = 2 cos((α+β)/2) cos((α−β)/2) yields, for α=(k+1)ϕ and β=(k−1)ϕ, the recurrence cos(k+1)ϕ = 2 cos ϕ cos kϕ − cos(k−1)ϕ. For ϕ_n = arccos(1/√n) one gets representations cos kϕ_n = A_k / n^{k/2} where A_k are integers not divisible by n and satisfy A_{k+1} = 2A_k − nA_{k−1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this integer recurrence to show that rationality of A(n) = (1/π) arccos(1/√n) would force integer divisibility contradictions for odd n ≥ 3, proving A(n) irrational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate ζ(2) via double integral by expanding geometric series
rubrics_metrics.description: I := ∫_0^1 ∫_0^1 1/(1−xy) dx dy; expand 1/(1−xy) = Σ_{n≥0} (xy)^n and integrate termwise to obtain I = Σ_{n≥1} 1/n^2 = ζ(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because integrand is positive and the integral converges, termwise integration is justified; this yields a double-integral representation of ζ(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate substitution and Jacobian use for double integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform substitutions x = x(u,v), y = y(u,v) when mapping is bijective and continuously differentiable, then transform integral via the Jacobian determinant d(x,y)/d(u,v). Example: u=(x+y)/2, v=(y−x)/2 has Jacobian 2, transforms domain and integrand symmetrically to evaluate I = π^2/6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit symmetry to reduce domain and simplify integrand (use arctan antiderivatives or other standard primitives). Compute Jacobian explicitly to account for area scaling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beukers–Calabi–Kolk substitution for splitting even/odd terms
rubrics_metrics.description: For J = ∫_0^1 ∫_0^1 1/(1−x^2 y^2) dx dy = Σ_{k≥0} 1/(2k+1)^2, introduce coordinates u := arccos((1−x^2)/(1−x^2 y^2)), v := arccos((1−y^2)/(1−x^2 y^2)), invertible with x = sin u / cos v, y = sin v / cos u; the Jacobian equals 1−x^2 y^2, transforming the integral into the area of triangle T (π^2/8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clever coordinate transforms tailored to the algebraic structure (here factoring 1−x^2 y^2) to reduce a complicated double integral to a simple geometric area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cotangent polynomial identity and coefficient comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: For n = 2m+1 and x = rπ/(2m+1) (r=1,..,m), expanding sin nx = (cos x + i sin x)^n and dividing by sin^n x produces a polynomial p(t) of degree m whose roots are t_r = cot^2(rπ/(2m+1)). Comparing coefficients yields Σ_{r=1}^m cot^2(rπ/(2m+1)) = 2m(2m−1)/6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate trigonometric identities into algebraic polynomials and compare coefficients to obtain exact finite sums of cotangent squares; then combine with inequalities to relate to ζ(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use cot^2 and csc^2 inequalities to sandwich 1/n^2
rubrics_metrics.description: For 0 < y < π/2, cot^2 y < 1/y^2 < csc^2 y. Apply this for y = rπ/(2m+1) and sum over r to obtain inequalities that squeeze partial sums of 1/n^2 between expressions tending to π^2/6 as m→∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This comparison method combined with explicit cot/csc sums yields an elementary convergence proof for Σ 1/n^2 = π^2/6.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare series tails with integrals for convergence/error estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: For the tail Σ_{n=m+1}^� 1/n^2 use integral comparisons: Σ_{n=m+1}^� 1/n^2 < ∫_m^� 1/t^2 dt = 1/m and Σ_{n=m+1}^� 1/n^2 > ∫_{m+1}^� 1/t^2 dt = 1/(m+1), with improved bounds using convexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard technique for bounding series remainder and estimating number of terms needed for a given decimal accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pearl Lemma for equidecomposability (integer-weight assignment)
rubrics_metrics.description: If P and Q are equidecomposable, then one can place positive numbers of pearls (assign positive integers) to all the segments of the decompositions P = P_1 ∪ ··· ∪ P_n and Q = Q_1 ∪ ··· ∪ Q_n so that each edge of a piece P_k receives the same number of pearls as the corresponding edge of Q_k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model segments with variables x_i (for P) and y_j (for Q) and set up integer-coefficient linear equations equating sums on corresponding edges: Σ_{i: s_i ⊆ e} x_i − Σ_{j: s'_j ⊆ e'} y_j = 0. Existence of positive real solution (the actual segment lengths) plus an integer-solution lemma (referenced) yields a positive integer solution; this provides an invariant obstructing non-equidecomposability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition/handling of segments in decompositions
rubrics_metrics.description: In a decomposition the edges of one piece may be subdivided by vertices or edges of other pieces; the pieces of this subdivision are called segments. In 2D any endpoint of a segment is a vertex; in 3D an endpoint may be a crossing of two edges. All interior points of a segment belong to the same set of piece-edges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When setting up linear constraints for pearl counts or other invariants, treat these segments as atomic units; keep track of how edges decompose into segments when forming equal-sum constraints.
